pleiades-nebula.name: Pleiades Nebula
pleiades-nebula.introduction: is the blue haze around the brightest stars of the Seven Sisters, about 440 light-years away in Taurus. It looks like the cloud the stars were born from, but it is not: the cluster is simply passing through a dusty patch of space. Its brightest part is also known as the Merope Nebula, or NGC 1435.

image.alt: The brightest Pleiades stars wrapped in veils of blue reflection nebulosity.
image.caption: NASA, ESA, AURA/Caltech, Palomar Observatory · visible light · released 2004
image.credit: NASA, ESA, AURA/Caltech, Palomar Observatory. Visible light, released 2004. Resized to 600 × 433 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

sections.title: A chance encounter
sections.text: The nebulosity was once taken for material left over from the cluster’s birth. At about 100 million years old, though, the cluster should have lost that dust long ago to the pressure of starlight. The cloud is an unrelated one, moving at about 18 km/s relative to the stars. Its dust lies mainly in two layers along our line of sight.

sections.title: Hidden in Merope’s glare
sections.text: Wilhelm Tempel discovered the nebula around Merope on October 19, 1859, with a 10.5 cm refractor. Its most intense knot, IC 349, is only half an arcminute wide and sits so close to the star that it stayed unseen until E. E. Barnard found it in November 1890.

orion-nebula.name: Orion Nebula
orion-nebula.introduction: is the nearest region of massive star formation to Earth, about 1,270 light-years away in Orion. It shines as the fuzzy middle “star” of Orion’s sword, visible to the naked eye even from light-polluted skies. It is also known as Messier 42 and NGC 1976.

image.alt: Glowing red, pink and brown clouds of the Orion Nebula around a bright core of young stars.
image.caption: NASA, ESA, M. Robberto (STScI/ESA) and the Hubble Orion Treasury Project Team · Hubble mosaic · released 2006

sections.title: The element that never was
sections.text: Observers long noticed a green tint in the nebula that no known spectral line could explain, so some astronomers proposed a new element called nebulium. The true source was doubly ionized oxygen, in a “forbidden” transition that needs a near-perfect vacuum. No laboratory of the time could reproduce it, but the near-collision-free gas of deep space provides it naturally.

sections.title: The first nebula ever photographed
sections.text: On September 30, 1880, Henry Draper exposed a dry plate for 51 minutes through an 11-inch refractor and made the first astronomical photograph of a nebula. In 1883, the amateur Andrew Ainslie Common took exposures of up to 60 minutes in his garden in Ealing, west London, and recorded detail too faint for the human eye.

sections.title: Planets in the making
sections.text: In 1993, the Hubble Space Telescope gave the major confirmation of protoplanetary disks, soon nicknamed proplyds, around the nebula’s young stars. Their dust grains are growing, the first step toward planets. In July 2025, Webb and ALMA observations caught a planetary system beginning to form around the protostar HOPS-315.

sections.title: A hollow in a dark cloud
sections.text: The light comes mainly from gas on the back wall of a cavity carved into a much larger molecular cloud by the young stars inside it. Theta-1 Orionis C does most of the work, emitting 3–4 times as much ionizing light as the next brightest star. That hollow is what lets us see the core stars at all.

sections.title: Missed by Galileo
sections.text: Neither Ptolemy, al-Sufi nor Galileo mentioned the nebula, although Galileo observed the surrounding stars with a telescope in 1610 and 1617. The first record of its nebulous nature is usually credited to Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc, on November 26, 1610. Its silence in older sources has led to speculation that its stars flared up.

ic-4592.name: Blue Horsehead Nebula
ic-4592.introduction: is a large blue reflection nebula about 470 light-years away in Scorpius, whose dust lanes outline the head and neck of a horse in wide-field photographs. It is lit by Nu Scorpii. It is also known as IC 4592 and vdB 100.

image.alt: A long blue cloud shaped like a horse’s head and neck among brown dust and dense star fields.
image.caption: Giuseppe Donatiello · visible light · 2023
image.credit: Giuseppe Donatiello. Visible light, 2023. Resized to 600 × 614 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: IC 4592 Blue Horsehead Nebula

sections.title: Seven stars for one lamp
sections.text: Nu Scorpii looks like a single fourth-magnitude star, but it is most likely a septuple system, made of two close groups separated by 41 arcseconds. Only one other seven-star system is known, AR Cassiopeiae, because such crowded systems tend to fall apart. Lying near the ecliptic, the star will next be occulted by Mercury on December 2, 2031.

ic-4601.name: IC 4601
ic-4601.introduction: is a pair of blue reflection nebulae around young stars about 430 light-years away in Scorpius, near its border with Ophiuchus. Its two parts are also catalogued as vdB 102 and vdB 103.

image.alt: Two bright stars embedded in streaks of blue reflection nebulosity.
image.caption: Adam Block/Mount Lemmon SkyCenter/University of Arizona · visible light · 2010
image.credit: Adam Block/Mount Lemmon SkyCenter/University of Arizona. Visible light, 2010. Resized to 600 × 392 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

sections.title: The lit corner of a dark river
sections.text: IC 4601 is the illuminated part of a large dark complex called B41, which runs north-east across the sky. Other parts of the same complex glow under other stars and appear as separate nebulae, among them IC 4592. The brightest star nearby, HD 147010, is a blue giant of about magnitude 7.4 whose light varies slightly.

ic-4603.name: IC 4603
ic-4603.introduction: is a reflection nebula at the western edge of the Rho Ophiuchi molecular cloud, about 450 light-years away in Ophiuchus. It is also known as vdB 105.

image.alt: Blue reflection nebula IC 4603 among dark lanes and red and orange clouds in the Rho Ophiuchi complex.
image.caption: Hwy37 · visible light · 2024
image.credit: Hwy37. Visible light, 2024. Resized to 600 × 412 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: Rho Ophiuchi core region with IC 4603

sections.title: A star inside its birth cloud
sections.text: The light comes from HD 147889, a B2 star wrapped in the gas in front of the cloud’s densest part. Dust filters its light and leaves its spectrum heavily reddened. Both its young age and its distance, the same as the cloud’s, show that it formed right here.

ic-4604.name: Rho Ophiuchi Nebula
ic-4604.introduction: is the blue glow around the multiple star Rho Ophiuchi, about 450 light-years away in Ophiuchus, on the edge of one of the nearest star-forming regions to the Solar System. It is also known as IC 4604 and vdB 106.

image.alt: Bright blue nebula around Rho Ophiuchi at right with the paler IC 4603 at left, separated by dark dust.
image.caption: Ivan Bok · visible light · 2016
image.credit: Ivan Bok. Visible light, 2016. Resized to 600 × 445 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

sections.title: “Strangeness and beauty”
sections.text: Burnham’s Celestial Handbook called this “a region of strangeness and beauty”. Dark lanes flow east from the nebula like black tentacles, ending about 11 degrees away near Xi Ophiuchi. E. E. Barnard described the view as a picture “almost unequalled in interest in the entire heavens”.

sections.title: A nursery next door
sections.text: Just to the south, the complex holds about 3,000 times the mass of the Sun at 13–22 K. More than 400 infrared sources crowd its densest cloud, L1688, including 16 protostars and about 200 T Tauri stars. It also gave astronomers the first brown dwarf identified in a star-forming region.

sections.title: The stars behind the glow
sections.text: Rho Ophiuchi’s central system has three blue stars: a close pair that circles every 88 days and a companion that takes about 2,400 years to orbit them. Together they dominate the radiation in the surrounding cloud.

ic-4605.name: IC 4605
ic-4605.introduction: is a blue reflection nebula about 410 light-years away in Scorpius, a little over a degree from Antares. It is a part of the Rho Ophiuchi cloud lit by the young star 22 Scorpii.

image.alt: Bright star 22 Scorpii in a blue haze, with orange dust and rich stars in the corners.
image.caption: Adam Block/Mount Lemmon SkyCenter/University of Arizona · visible light · 2015
image.credit: Adam Block/Mount Lemmon SkyCenter/University of Arizona. Visible light, 2015. Resized to 600 × 601 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

sections.title: Too gentle to ionize
sections.text: The B3 star 22 Scorpii sends too little ultraviolet light to strip electrons from the gas around it. The cloud therefore only reflects the star’s light, and its glow stays blue instead of turning hydrogen red. A few arcminutes to the north-east begins LDN 1689, one of the cloud’s two great dark filaments, home to the much-studied forming multiple star IRAS 16293-2422.

ic-4606.name: Antares Nebula
ic-4606.introduction: is the vast golden cloud lit by Antares, the red supergiant at the heart of Scorpius, about 550 light-years away. Dust scatters the star’s orange light without changing its color, which sets this nebula apart from the blue ones around it. It is also known as IC 4606 and vdB 107.

image.alt: Brilliant Antares in a golden cloud of dust crossed by deep red lanes.
image.caption: Adam Block/Steward Observatory/University of Arizona · visible light
image.credit: Adam Block/Steward Observatory/University of Arizona. Visible light. Resized to 600 × 600 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

sections.title: A red lamp in front of a dark cloud
sections.text: Antares is the brightest and most evolved member of the Scorpius–Centaurus association, the nearest group of its kind to the Sun. It lies on the rim of the Upper Scorpius subgroup, whose stars have a mean age of 11 million years, and it lights part of the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex in its foreground.

sections.title: A filament with no stars behind it
sections.text: The cloud is connected to LDN 1689, one of the largest parts of the Rho Ophiuchi cloud. To the north that dust forms a long filament running east. It is unlit and cannot be seen directly, but it stands out even in small instruments as a band with no background stars at all.

vdb-101.name: vdB 101
vdb-101.introduction: is a faint reflection nebula about 420 light-years away in Scorpius, lit by the sixth-magnitude orange giant HD 146834. With a cool star for a lamp, it lacks the strong blue of its neighbors. It is a small part of the same dust that forms the nearby IC 4601.

vdb-109.name: vdB 109
vdb-109.introduction: is a very faint veil of reflecting dust about 390 light-years away in Ophiuchus, spread across 36 arcminutes of sky around the yellow giant 24 Scorpii. The star may only lie along the same line of sight.

sections.title: A Scorpius star in Ophiuchus
sections.text: John Flamsteed placed 24 Scorpii in Scorpius. When the constellation borders were fixed in 1930, the star ended up in Ophiuchus, so its name no longer matches its address. It is a luminous giant, probably fusing helium in its core, with 22 times the Sun’s radius and 208 times its light.

vdb-111.name: vdB 111
vdb-111.introduction: is a small blue reflection nebula about 470 light-years away in northern Ophiuchus, next to a star that pulses. V2112 Ophiuchi, a Delta Scuti variable of the sixth magnitude, changes by about 0.2 magnitudes every four and a half hours.

vdb-25.name: vdB 25
vdb-25.introduction: is an extremely faint wisp of reflecting dust about 460 light-years away in Taurus, close to the yellow giant HD 26514 and in the same part of the sky as the Taurus clouds. The star is itself a binary whose fainter partner lies only one arcsecond away.

source.title: CDS and ESA: DSS colored survey

vdb-26.name: vdB 26
vdb-26.introduction: is a small, very blue reflection nebula about 470 light-years away in Taurus, south of the main Taurus clouds. Its light comes from HD 26676, a blue-white B8 star at magnitude 6.2, just bright enough for the naked eye under dark skies.

vdb-27.name: vdB 27
vdb-27.introduction: is a faint reflection nebula about 450 light-years away in Taurus, on the edge of the dark cloud Barnard 214. It is lit by RY Tauri, a young star whose changes in brightness also make the nebula vary.

image.alt: The young star RY Tauri with a faint fan of nebulosity above it.
image.caption: Digitized Sky Survey 2 · STScI/NASA, colored by CDS · visible-light survey composite

sections.title: A star Henrietta Leavitt caught flickering
sections.text: Henrietta Swan Leavitt’s discovery that RY Tauri is variable was reported in 1907. Over a decade the star changes by 2–3 magnitudes as it shines through the uneven inner part of its disk, and jets of gas stream from it. A giant planet on a 0.2 au orbit has been suspected since 2021.

hinds-variable-nebula.name: Hind’s Variable Nebula
hinds-variable-nebula.introduction: is a small cloud that fades and comes back, about 470 light-years away in Taurus. It is lit by T Tauri, the star that gave its name to a whole class of newborn stars. John Russell Hind discovered it on October 11, 1852. It is also known as NGC 1555.

image.alt: A small fiery orange nebula beside the young star T Tauri, in a field of dark brown dust.
image.caption: Adam Block/Mount Lemmon SkyCenter/University of Arizona · visible light · 2010
image.credit: Adam Block/Mount Lemmon SkyCenter/University of Arizona. Visible light, 2010. Resized to 600 × 400 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

sections.title: The nebula that vanished
sections.text: By the 1860s the nebula had faded from view for nearly everyone, including Hind. In 1868 Otto Struve, with one of the world’s most powerful telescopes, lost it too, but found a new patch about four arcminutes to the west. Over the next 10–20 years that “Struve’s Lost Nebula” faded and Hind’s nebula returned.

sections.title: A great dimming under way
sections.text: T Tauri is really three young stars. The southern pair is hidden by a ring of dust, and that ring is drifting in front of the northern star. Between 2015 and 2024 the northern star faded by about 2 magnitudes, which may be the start of a dimming lasting 60–70 years or more.

vdb-7.name: vdB 7
vdb-7.introduction: is a small, faint reflection nebula in Cassiopeia, a few arcminutes south of the sixth-magnitude eclipsing binary RZ Cassiopeiae. The bright star may be a bystander: the nebula’s real source of light may be a much fainter star of the eleventh magnitude. Its distance of about 210 light-years, measured from RZ Cassiopeiae, is therefore only a rough guide.

image.alt: A very bright blue-white star above a faint patch of nebulosity.
image.caption: Digitized Sky Survey 2 · STScI/NASA, colored by CDS · visible-light survey composite · contrast stretched

vdb-129.name: vdB 129
vdb-129.introduction: is a large, faint patch of reflecting dust about 230 light-years away in Aquila, more than three times the width of the full Moon. It lies toward Theta Aquilae, a third-magnitude star with a close companion, although the link between star and dust is not certain.

image.alt: The bright star Theta Aquilae in a rich star field with very faint patches of nebulosity.
image.caption: M. Amari · visible light · 2011
image.credit: M. Amari. Visible light, 2011. Resized to 600 × 400 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

vdb-156.name: vdB 156
vdb-156.introduction: is a very large, very faint reflection nebula about 350 light-years away in Andromeda, spanning some 3 degrees of sky around the star Omicron Andromedae, a width of six full Moons.

sections.title: A runaway with a horse’s name
sections.text: Omicron Andromedae is a multiple system of at least three stars, moving fast enough through space to count as a runaway. Its brightest star varies between magnitudes 3.58 and 3.78. Its name, Alfarasalkamil, approved in May 2025, recalls the Complete Horse of traditional Arabic skies.

sh-2-27.name: Sh 2-27
sh-2-27.introduction: is one of the closest known emission nebulae, a huge, faint sphere of glowing hydrogen about 440 light-years away in Ophiuchus. At least 8 degrees across, it would cover the width of 16 full Moons. It is lit by the star Zeta Ophiuchi and is also known as the Cobold Nebula.

image.alt: A large rounded pink cloud of ionized hydrogen behind green and blue molecular clouds, in false color.
image.caption: Tk833 · hydrogen-alpha and continuum, false color · 2025
image.credit: Tk833. Hydrogen-alpha and continuum, false color, 2025. Resized to 600 × 399 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: SH2-27 in H-alpha and continuum

sections.title: A runaway from a supernova
sections.text: Zeta Ophiuchi, the nearest O-type star to the Solar System, moves through space at about 30 km/s and plows a bow shock through the dust ahead of it. It may once have had a massive companion that exploded. The pulsar PSR B1929+10 could be what remains of that star, because it was thrown from the same group of stars on a path that fits.

sections.title: A star hiding behind dust
sections.text: Dust blocks much of Zeta Ophiuchi’s light. Seen clearly, this magnitude 2.6 star would shine at about magnitude 1.5, among the brightest in the night sky. It also spins near its breaking point, possibly once a day, with a surface that ranges from about 39,000 K at the poles to 30,700 K at the equator.

sh-2-7.name: Sh 2-7
sh-2-7.introduction: is a faint, patchy cloud of glowing gas around Delta Scorpii, about 490 light-years away in Scorpius. It frames one of the bright stars in the scorpion’s head, and the star’s glare makes the nebula hard to observe.

sections.title: The star that changed Scorpius
sections.text: Delta Scorpii, or Dschubba, was long considered steady. In June 2000 Sebastian Otero saw that it had brightened by a tenth of a magnitude, and it has reached at least magnitude 1.6 since, changing the familiar look of the constellation. It is throwing off luminous gas from its equator.

sections.title: What a supernova left behind
sections.text: Sh 2-7 and its neighbors are remnants of the giant cloud that formed the stars of this group about 5 million years ago. A supernova about 1.5 million years ago helped break that cloud apart, leaving the scattered patches seen around these stars today.

abell-35.name: Abell 35
abell-35.introduction: looks like a planetary nebula but probably is not one. About 450 light-years away in Hydra, it seems to be ordinary interstellar gas, lit up by a hot white dwarf that happens to be passing through. It is also known as Sh 2-313.

image.alt: A faint round red shell with a pale blue-green bow shock near its bright central star.
image.caption: Jerry Macon · hydrogen-alpha, oxygen and RGB filters · 2021
image.credit: Jerry Macon. Hydrogen-alpha, oxygen and RGB filters, 2021. Resized to 600 × 424 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

sections.title: A pair too light to make a nebula
sections.text: The central star turned out to be two. The visible one is a fast-spinning G-type subgiant, and in ultraviolet light astronomers found a white dwarf at about 80,000 K. With a mass of only 0.48 Suns, the white dwarf seems too small to have made a planetary nebula. The pair moves at about 150 km/s, which drives the bow shock at the nebula’s center.

sh-2-216.name: Sh 2-216
sh-2-216.introduction: is the nearest known planetary nebula, about 420 light-years away in Perseus. At about 100 arcminutes across, it spans more than three times the width of the full Moon, but it is so faint that it needs deep exposures to show at all.

image.alt: A huge round orange-red shell with streaky filaments and a paler center, in false color.
image.caption: Manuel Peitsch · narrowband filters, false color · 2023
image.credit: Manuel Peitsch. Narrowband filters, false color, 2023. Resized to 600 × 418 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

sections.title: Old, slow and off-center
sections.text: At roughly 600,000 years, this is one of the oldest planetary nebulae known. Its gas is being compressed and slowed by the interstellar medium along its eastern edge, while its white dwarf keeps moving on its original path. As a result, the star no longer sits at the center of its own nebula.

sections.title: Two decades as the wrong kind of nebula
sections.text: Stewart Sharpless listed the object in 1959 as an H II region, misled by its enormous size and low surface brightness. Its emission lines suggested a planetary nebula in 1981, and its white dwarf was confirmed in 1985.

lambda-orionis-nebula.name: Lambda Orionis Nebula
lambda-orionis-nebula.introduction: is a giant bubble of glowing gas about 1,330 light-years away in Orion, some 6 degrees across, surrounding the blue star that marks the Hunter’s head. A ring of dust and molecular gas encloses it. It is also known as Sh 2-264 and, for its shape, the Angelfish Nebula.

image.alt: A vast pink ring of glowing gas around the star Lambda Orionis, with orange Betelgeuse at lower left.
image.caption: Rogelio Bernal Andreo; crop by Lithopsian · visible light · 2017
image.credit: Rogelio Bernal Andreo; crop by Lithopsian. Visible light, 2017. Resized to 600 × 437 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

sections.title: Blown out by a blast?
sections.text: The surrounding molecular ring has been interpreted as the mark of a supernova that exploded about one million years ago. In that picture, the blast hit the gas around a young star cluster, dispersed the parent cloud and pushed what remained into the ring seen today.

sections.title: Disks under fire
sections.text: Inside the ring lies Collinder 69, a cluster about five million years old that also goes by the name Aunt Margaret’s Mirror. A quarter of its low-mass stars and 40% of its smaller objects still have disks around them. Two of those disks are being evaporated by the fierce light of Lambda Orionis itself.

sh-2-277.name: Flame Nebula and IC 434
sh-2-277.introduction: is a glowing region on the edge of the Orion B cloud, about 1,310 light-years away, that holds two of the most photographed sights in the sky: the Flame Nebula (NGC 2024) and the red curtain of IC 434, against which the dark Horsehead Nebula stands out.

image.alt: The dark Horsehead against a red curtain of IC 434, the golden Flame Nebula at left and bright Alnitak above.
image.caption: Gianni Lacroce · visible light and hydrogen-alpha · 2023
image.credit: Gianni Lacroce. Visible light and hydrogen-alpha, 2023. Resized to 600 × 409 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: Horsehead Nebula and Flame Nebula

sections.title: A curtain for the Horsehead
sections.text: Williamina Fleming discovered the Horsehead in 1888 on a photographic plate at Harvard College Observatory. It is a dark pillar of dust pushing out of Orion B, visible only because IC 434 glows behind it. Sigma Orionis supplies the ultraviolet light that makes that curtain of hydrogen shine.

sections.title: Fire hidden behind dust
sections.text: The Flame looks like the work of nearby Alnitak, but that star is unrelated. Its true engine is IRS 2b, a hot O-type star buried inside the nebula behind thick dust. Around it lie an estimated 800 young stars, most of them with disks, that can only be studied well in infrared light and X-rays.

sections.title: Named for Horace Hedd
sections.text: In Isaac Asimov’s 1951 novel The Stars, Like Dust, two characters argue over the Horsehead’s name. One knows it comes from its shape. The other, raised on another planet, is sure that it honors Horace Hedd, the first man to enter it.

california-nebula.name: California Nebula
california-nebula.introduction: is a long ribbon of glowing hydrogen about 1,330 light-years away in Perseus, almost 2.5 degrees from end to end and shaped like the US state it is named after. E. E. Barnard discovered it in 1884. It is also known as NGC 1499.

image.alt: A long pale ribbon of glowing gas with dark dust knots, shaped like the US state of California.
image.caption: Taavi Niittee/Tõrva Astronomy Club · narrowband filters · 2024
image.credit: Taavi Niittee/Tõrva Astronomy Club. Narrowband filters, 2024. Resized to 600 × 300 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: California nebula from Estonia

sections.title: Overhead in California
sections.text: By coincidence, the California Nebula passes straight overhead in central California, because that region’s latitude matches the nebula’s declination. Even so, its surface is so dim that it is very hard to see by eye, even with a hydrogen filter under dark skies. Galaxies in the Perseus–Pisces Supercluster show through it from far behind.

sections.title: Lit by a runaway
sections.text: The gas glows under the radiation of Xi Persei, or Menkib, one of the hottest stars visible to the naked eye. With about 30 times the Sun’s mass and a surface of 35,000 K, it radiates some 263,000 times the Sun’s power. It sits 200 parsecs from the center of its group of young stars and may be a runaway.

flaming-star-nebula.name: Flaming Star Nebula
flaming-star-nebula.introduction: is a cloud of glowing gas and reflecting dust about 1,270 light-years away in Auriga, lit by a star that does not belong to it. The runaway star AE Aurigae is only passing through. It is also known as IC 405 and Caldwell 31.

image.alt: Rippling red hydrogen clouds and blue dust around the bright star AE Aurigae.
image.caption: Adam Block/Mount Lemmon SkyCenter/University of Arizona · visible light · 2016
image.credit: Adam Block/Mount Lemmon SkyCenter/University of Arizona. Visible light, 2016. Resized to 600 × 596 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

sections.title: Thrown out of Orion
sections.text: AE Aurigae was not born in this cloud. Its path traces back to the Trapezium cluster in the Orion Nebula, where a collision between two pairs of stars seems to have flung it out about two million years ago, along with Mu Columbae. Today it plows through the nebula at high speed, driving a bow shock.

sh-2-1.name: Sh 2-1
sh-2-1.introduction: is a faint cloud about 2.5 degrees across, about 590 light-years away in Scorpius, arcing around the bright star Pi Scorpii. It both glows and reflects, and it is a remnant of the giant cloud that formed the blue stars in the scorpion’s head.

image.alt: The bright star Pi Scorpii beside pale blue arcs and dark lanes of dust.
